name: Adam Smith
description: Scottish philosopher and economist associated with commercial liberty, moral sympathy and public institutions.
scope: Public positions and conduct during the specified period; this represents the individual rather than all party members or citizens.

axes.brief: Accountable law and criticism of political privilege supply representative-government context.
axes.counter: Modern universal suffrage and referendums are analogies rather than explicit institutional proposals.

axes.brief: Natural liberty and protection against arbitrary rule constrained state interference.
axes.counter: Civil justice and public order remained legitimate functions; personal drug policy is inferred.

axes.brief: Commercial society and criticism of prejudice supply cultural-tolerance context.
axes.counter: Eighteenth-century national and colonial assumptions limit modern multicultural translations.

axes.brief: Free labour movement and criticism of settlement restrictions support mobility.
axes.counter: Poor-law settlement criticism does not precisely settle modern refugee or welfare policy.

axes.brief: Defence was a legitimate public duty while war and empire imposed heavy costs.
axes.counter: A standing army could be preferable in advanced societies; he was not an absolute pacifist.

axes.brief: National justice and defence coexisted with commercial cooperation.
axes.counter: Modern binding international agencies and shared currency lack direct equivalents.

axes.brief: Private commercial enterprise was preferred in ordinary production.
axes.counter: Public works and education could be publicly supported where private incentives were inadequate.

axes.brief: Criticism of mercantilism favoured open trade and competition.
axes.counter: Defence-related navigation restrictions and strategic retaliation were qualified exceptions.

reasons.4: The defence-related navigation exception supplies a real counterweight to cheaper imports. Essential goods include both ordinary necessities and strategic defence supplies, making a conditional response to this broad formulation plausible.
reasons.10: He accepted retaliatory duties where they were likely to produce removal of a foreign barrier but rejected costly retaliation without that prospect. The question omits the condition, so a mixed response is preferable.

axes.brief: Market prices and decentralised enterprise were preferred.
axes.counter: Banking regulation, public works and education qualify a maximal laissez-faire interpretation.

axes.brief: Tax fairness and public revenue coexisted with acceptance of commercial income differences.
axes.counter: Some taxes on the rich could exceed simple proportionality; he did not advocate modern comprehensive transfers.

reasons.4: His discussion of taxes on expensive housing permits richer citizens to contribute more than proportionately. Agreement is qualified because it does not establish every modern substantially progressive income-tax schedule.

axes.brief: Civil authority and competing religious sects limited ecclesiastical domination.
axes.counter: Historical established churches and moral education qualify contemporary complete separation.

axes.brief: Moral propriety and conventional family expectations reflected eighteenth-century context.
axes.counter: Sympathy and criticism of privilege challenge a blanket endorsement of every inherited custom.

axes.brief: Commercial improvement and productive innovation were valued.
axes.counter: Modern neural or embryo enhancement has no direct counterpart.

axes.brief: Local financing could suit local public works while national defence and justice remained.
axes.counter: Modern constitutional secession and Indigenous sovereignty are uncertain translations.

axes.brief: Habit, education and social interaction shaped conduct alongside natural sympathy and passions.
axes.counter: Universal human dispositions are not evidence of inherited race differences.
